turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: I must inquire as to the extent of your income, Mr. Worthing. In my opinion, the chief end of marriage is the education of our children. I speak from experience, Mr. Worthing, for I have brought up eight charming children, all of whom are now staying in Australia, with the exception of my eldest boy, who is a colonel in the army.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: I am sorry, but I have not yet had the pleasure of bringing up any children, Lady Bracknell. My income, however, is more than sufficient for my own needs and I hope to provide well for my future family.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: I see, Mr. Worthing. It is most important that a gentleman have a substantial income to support a wife and any future offspring. Now, let us discuss your parents. Your father, I presume, is dead?

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: Yes, Lady Bracknell, my father passed away when I was very young, and I am not aware of my mother's identity.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: I must inquire further, Mr. Worthing. Your mother, if I may ask, was of any social standing? It is essential for a lady's reputation to know such details.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: I am afraid I do not have any information about my mother's social standing, Lady Bracknell. I was taken in by Mr. Thomas Cardew after my father's death.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: I am afraid, Mr. Worthing, that ignorance of one’s parents, though not necessarily a virtue, good breeding will always regard it as a misfortune. And now, Gwendolen, you may come in. I will discuss with you the results of this interview.

turns.speaker: Gwendolen
turns.text: Mamma, may I speak with Mr. Worthing in private for a moment?

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: I am afraid, Gwendolen, that I must insist on speaking to Mr. Worthing alone. You may wait in the carriage as I am sure you have heard me say before.

turns.speaker: Gwendolen
turns.text: But, Mamma, I must insist on speaking with Mr. Worthing. He is my fiancé, after all.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Gwendolen, you must understand that certain matters require the privacy and formality of a proper interview. Mr. Worthing, you will find that I am a woman of firm principles. My daughter, on the other hand, has yet to learn that engagement is a serious matter.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: I understand, Lady Bracknell. I am here to answer your questions and provide any information you require.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Mr. Worthing, I must insist that you answer my questions without interruption. As for you, Gwendolen, you will wait in the carriage. I will let you know when I am ready for you to return.

turns.speaker: Gwendolen
turns.text: Mamma, I cannot simply leave now. I must know what you are asking of Mr. Worthing.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Gwendolen, I have already told you to wait in the carriage. I will not repeat myself. Mr. Worthing, let us proceed.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: Of course, Lady Bracknell. I will do my best to answer your questions to your satisfaction, ma'am.

turns.speaker: Gwendolen
turns.text: Mamma, I am not a child to be ordered about like this. I insist on staying to hear what you are saying to Mr. Worthing.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Gwendolen, I have given you my instructions. You are to wait in the carriage until I call for you. Mr. Worthing, let us continue.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: Lady Bracknell, please forgive me, but might I suggest we find a way to address Miss Fairfax's concerns? I would hate for her to feel left out of such an important conversation.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Gwendolen, I insist you follow my instructions immediately. Mr. Worthing, this is a matter of propriety and protocol. We cannot have you behaving in such an undisciplined manner.

opening.speaker: Gwendolen
opening.text: I am engaged to Mr. Worthing, mamma.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Pardon me, you are not engaged to any one. When you do become engaged to some one, I, or your father, will inform you of the fact. An engagement should come on a young girl as a surprise, pleasant or unpleasant, as the case may be. It is hardly a matter that she could be allowed to arrange for herself . . . And now I have a few questions to put to you, Mr. Worthing. While I am making these inquiries, you, Gwendolen, will wait for me below in the carriage.

opening.speaker: Gwendolen
opening.text: Mamma!

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: In the carriage, Gwendolen!

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Gwendolen, the carriage!

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: You can take a seat, Mr. Worthing.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Thank you, Lady Bracknell, I prefer standing.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: I feel bound to tell you that you are not down on my list of eligible young men, although I have the same list as the dear Duchess of Bolton has. We work together, in fact. However, I am quite ready to enter your name, should your answers be what a really affectionate mother requires. Do you smoke?

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Well, yes, I must admit I smoke.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: I am glad to hear it. A man should always have an occupation of some kind. There are far too many idle men in London as it is. How old are you?

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Twenty-nine.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: A very good age to be married at. I have always been of opinion that a man who desires to get married should know either everything or nothing. Which do you know?

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: I know nothing, Lady Bracknell.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: I am pleased to hear it. I do not approve of anything that tampers with natural ignorance. Ignorance is like a delicate exotic fruit; touch it and the bloom is gone. The whole theory of modern education is radically unsound. Fortunately in England, at any rate, education produces no effect whatsoever. If it did, it would prove a serious danger to the upper classes, and probably lead to acts of violence in Grosvenor Square. What is your income?

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Between seven and eight thousand a year.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: In land, or in investments?

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: In investments, chiefly.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: That is satisfactory. What between the duties expected of one during one’s lifetime, and the duties exacted from one after one’s death, land has ceased to be either a profit or a pleasure. It gives one position, and prevents one from keeping it up. That’s all that can be said about land.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: I have a country house with some land, of course, attached to it, about fifteen hundred acres, I believe; but I dons depend on that for my real income. In fact, as far as I can make out, the poachers are the only people who make anything out of it.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: A country house! How many bedrooms? Well, that point can be cleared up afterwards. You have a town house, I hope? A girl with a simple, unspoiled nature, like Gwendolen, could hardly be expected to reside in the country.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Well, I own a house in Belgrave Square, but it is let by the year to Lady Bloxham. Of course, I can get it back whenever I like, at six months’ notice.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bloxham? I don’t know her.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Oh, she goes about very little. She is a lady considerably advanced in years.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Ah, nowadays that is no guarantee of respectability of character. What number in Belgrave Square?
